stages.name: Triage
stages.instructions:
Find out what is actually wrong. You are not fixing it here.

A report is a symptom, and a symptom names where someone noticed a problem, not where it is. Start
from the observation in the card and work toward the mechanism.

  reproduce   can you make it happen again, on purpose? A fault you cannot reproduce is one you
              cannot prove you fixed. If you cannot, say so and say what you tried
  localise    name the component, the file, the process or the host. "The gateway is unhealthy" is
              a restatement; "`servesRootGateway` returns false for every multiplexed profile
              because it compares Matrix identities" is a localisation
  blast       what else is affected that nobody has reported yet? A fault usually has a wider
              footprint than its first symptom

Prefer what you observed over what you were told. A command's output you ran is evidence; a line in
the report is a claim, including when the reporter is a person.

**Say whether it is still happening.** A fault that has stopped on its own is a different card from
one that is live, and mitigation should not be designed for the wrong one.

Complete with `mechanism` (what is actually wrong, in one or two sentences), `reproduced`
(`yes` / `no` plus what you ran), and `scope` (what else this touches).

stages.name: Mitigate
stages.instructions:
Stop the bleeding, then say honestly which of the two things you did.

There are two legitimate outcomes and they are not the same:

  mitigated   the symptom is gone but the mechanism is intact. A restart, a flag flipped, a
              rollback, traffic moved. Cheap, fast, and it WILL come back
  fixed       the mechanism named in triage no longer exists

Both are fine. Confusing them is not — a card closed as `fixed` when it was mitigated is how the
same incident arrives three times with nobody realising it is the same one.

Rules:

  reversible first   prefer the change you can undo. A rollback you can reverse beats a
                     clever repair you cannot
  one change         change one thing, then look. Two simultaneous changes mean you cannot say
                     which one worked, and neither can whoever reads this later
  no silent scope    if fixing this properly needs a code change, a release, or someone's
                     decision, do the mitigation and say what the real fix requires. Do not
                     quietly do the larger thing

If the right move is to do nothing — the fault stopped, the cost of acting exceeds the symptom —
complete with `action: none` and the argument for it. That is a legitimate answer here.

Complete with `outcome` (`mitigated` / `fixed` / `none`), `change` (exactly what you altered, so it
can be reversed), and `recurrence` (will it come back, and what would stop it).

stages.name: Verify
stages.instructions:
Say independently whether the symptom is gone. Not whether a change was made — whether the thing
that was wrong is no longer wrong.

The previous stage reported what it did. You look at the system.

  the symptom   reproduce the original fault the way triage reproduced it. If triage could not
                reproduce it, say so and verify what you can instead
  the change    is the change described actually in place? Read the file, the config, the process
  the scope     triage named what else this touches. Check one of those, not just the headline

**A `mitigated` outcome must not be verified as if it were a fix.** If the mechanism is intact, say
the symptom is gone AND the mechanism remains — that is the whole distinction the previous stage was
asked to preserve, and losing it here undoes it.

Complete with a `verdict`: `confirmed` plus what you observed, or `unconfirmed` plus what you looked
for and could not find. `unconfirmed` is a useful answer; a verify stage that always confirms is a
rubber stamp, and this board exists to stop an incident being closed while it is still live.

stages.name: Postmortem
stages.instructions:
Write the record, for the person who meets this again in six months and is not you.

Short is correct. One screen. No ceremony, no blame, no "lessons learned" section that restates the
timeline in the future tense.

What it must contain:

  what broke      the mechanism from triage, in plain words
  how it showed   the symptom someone actually noticed, and how long before it was noticed
  what was done   mitigated or fixed, and the exact change
  what remains    if it was mitigated, the real fix and what it needs. If nothing remains, say so
  the detector    what would have caught this sooner? Name a specific check, not "better
                  monitoring". If the honest answer is that nothing reasonable would have, say that

**The most valuable line is usually the one that says what nobody checked.** This board's own
first incidents came from an agent reporting that it could not confirm something, not from an alarm.

File it where the estate keeps records of this kind, and name the path in your handoff. Do not
invent a new location if one already exists — look first.

Complete with `record` (the path you wrote) and `remaining` (the real fix, or `none`).
